name: AI Cybersecurity and Governance
description: AI is no longer just answering questions. It is booking flights, reading email, interacting with other systems, and increasingly acting on your behalf. As AI shifts from passive assistant to autonomous agent, the opportunities are growing, but so are the risks.In AI Cybersecurity and Governance, you’ll connect lessons from major historical data breaches to emerging vulnerabilities in generative and agentic AI. Through real-world cases, you’ll examine threats including deepfake fraud, prompt injection, model extraction, Shadow AI, and attacks on AI systems. You’ll also explore governance frameworks such as ISO 42001, the Secure AI Framework (SAIF), and AIUC-1, as well as emerging AI regulations and their implications for organizations. No prerequisites or deeply technical background are required.Key BenefitsRecognize Breach Patterns: Examine recurring managerial and technical causes behind major cybersecurity breaches.Understand AI Risk: Distinguish the capabilities, autonomy levels, and representative threats associated with traditional machine learning, generative AI, and agentic AI.Assess Emerging Threats: Explore deepfakes, hallucinations, prompt injection, adversarial attacks, model extraction, and Shadow AI.Apply Security Safeguards: Examine Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), AI inventories, and AI Bill of Materials approaches for managing AI-related risk.Evaluate Governance Frameworks: Compare ISO 42001, SAIF, and AIUC-1 in the context of organizational AI governance.Examine Regulation: Analyze how AI regulations and liability considerations shape organizational deployment decisions.Learning OutcomesBy the end of this course, learners will be able to:Identify recurring managerial and technical root causes behind major historical breaches.Describe the expanded attack surface associated with generative and agentic AI.Analyze real-world AI-specific attacks that can affect organizational AI systems.Evaluate leading AI governance frameworks and regulatory mandates.Apply a decision-ready lens to AI risk management, including AI-BOM, HITL, and regulatory mapping.Whether you are evaluating an AI system, overseeing its adoption, or helping shape how it is used, you’ll develop a clearer framework for recognizing where new capabilities introduce new risks. You’ll also gain a practical lens for weighing security, governance, and regulatory considerations as AI becomes more deeply embedded in organizational decision-making.
